# Improving sampling: fixing an over-specified model

Sometimes the chains misbehave. We might see high R-hat values, tiny ESS and trace plots that wander and drift apart. In this module we'll look at some different strategies to improve the quality of MCMC sampling. Efficient sampling means you'll get accurate estimation of the posteriors in a shorter amount of time. 

## The data

We use `random-effects.csv`. This is benthic-cover survey from the same Kia Province reefs you met with the fish counts. Each row is one transect, and `cover` is the per-cent cover of branching *Acropora* coral. There are several transects per site, so `site` is a natural grouping variable for random effects.

## A broken model

Here is a model that tries to give every site its own free mean, on top of a global intercept, with very diffuse priors:

```
model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    cover[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    log(lambda[i]) <- alpha + beta[site[i]]
  }
  alpha ~ dnorm(0, 1000)
  for (j in 1:J) {
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, 1000)
  }
}
```

Set `J` to the number of sites (20) alongside `N` in the constants, then fit it. The diagnostics will be dreadful. You will notice the trace plots drift and wander and different chains don't converge on the same distribution (tick the 'show array parameters' button if you want to see traces for each `beta`).  R-hat for `alpha` and the `beta[j]` will be huge, and ESS be in the single digits.

## Fix 1: A new type of sampler

In FANGS there are two ways to draw *samples* from a model's posterior. See the option for the **Sampler engine**, in the sampler settings.

- **Standard** updates one parameter at a time. It works for any model FANGS can
  parse, which is why it's the default.
- **Blocked** updates all the fixed coefficients together, and all the group
  effects at once, and it makes moves that shift $\alpha$ up while shifting
  every $\beta_j$ down by the same amount — travelling *along* the ridge from
  the section above instead of crawling across it. It applies to GLMMs: a
  normal, Poisson or binomial response with `dnorm` priors on the coefficients.

Use **Blocked** whenever you're fitting a mixed-effects model, and especially
with many groups or more than a few hundred rows. On the 50-row example dataset
it runs about 100× faster, and the gain in *accuracy per second* is larger still
— because of the $\alpha$ ↔ $\beta_j$ ridge the standard engine needs roughly
900× more time to pin the intercept down as precisely.

Two things to be clear about:

- It targets the **same posterior**. This is a speed and mixing improvement, not
  a different model, and not a different answer.
- It **does not fix an over-specified model.** A genuinely non-identifiable
  model still has bad R-hat and ESS on either engine, because the problem is in
  the model, not the algorithm. Fix the model first (Fixes 1 and 2); then pick
  the engine.

If your model isn't one the blocked engine supports, FANGS quietly falls back to
Standard and tells you so in the status bar.

Re-run your model using the blocked engine. You will see the chains behave better, however the posteriors on most of the parameters are very wide. Then look at the 'Joint' tab, notice how samples for many pairs of `alpha` and `beta` params are a perfect negative correlation. This trading-off of parameter values is indicative of a **non-identifiable** model. 

## Non-identifiability

Non-identifiability is a common problem, but it's not always that obvious. Here's a really obvious example to start you off. 

Consider the linear predictor: $\log(\lambda_i) = \alpha + \beta_{\text{site}[i]}$. You can add any constant $c$ to $\alpha$ and subtract the same $c$ from *every* $\beta_j$, and the predictions are completely unchanged:

$$
(\alpha + c) + (\beta_j - c) = \alpha + \beta_j
$$

So the data can nail each sum $\alpha + \beta_j$, but never $\alpha$ and the $\beta_j$ separately — there are infinitely many equally good answers along a ridge. The two diffuse `dnorm(0, 1000)` priors do nothing to break the tie, so the sampler slides up and down that ridge forever. That is what a high R-hat and tiny ESS are telling you.

So our first intution was to try a new sampling algorithm. But often when you have problems with getting the chains to converge, it is becuase the model is asking the data to estimate something it **cannot**. This is an *over-specified* model. Often, the fix to look at how you are building the model and the priors. Othertimes, you might just be asking too much to fit the model you want to the data you have. 

::: callout-tip
The Folk Theorem of Statistical Computing (Gelman 2008): "When you have computational problems, often there’s a problem with your model. "
:::

## Fix 2: partial pooling and sensible priors

Back to our model of reefs. Make the site effects deviations around the global mean, drawn from a shared distribution whose width $\sigma_b$ the model estimates. Anchoring them at zero identifies $\alpha$ as the grand mean, and the shared prior pools information across sites:

```
model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    cover[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    log(lambda[i]) <- alpha + b[site[i]]
  }
  for (j in 1:J) {
    b[j] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
  }
  alpha   ~ dnorm(0, 10)
  sigma.b ~ dunif(0, 10)
}
```

Don't forget to re-enter J=20 before running the model. 

Two changes fixed our issue:

1. **Identifiability** — the `b[j]` are centred on 0 with a shared, estimated SD, so they can no longer trade off freely against `alpha`.
2. **Sensible priors** — `dnorm(0, 10)` on the log-scale intercept and a bounded `dunif(0, 10)` on $\sigma_b$ are weakly informative rather than too wide.

Refit and then check the posteriors. We are getting much more precise estimates of the parameters now. Check also the Joint tab. You will still see parameters trading-off, but not as strongly as before. 

## Fix 3: Reparameterisation

In hierarchical models the group SD $\sigma_b$ and the group effects $b_j$ are strongly coupled, creating a funnel-shaped posterior that is hard to sample (the "centred" parameterisation). A **non-centred** form decouples them:

```
for (j in 1:J) {
  z[j] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  b[j] <- sigma.b * z[j]
}
```

Making this change can, at times, improve the geometry of the joint posterior such that it is easier to sample. In this case it doesn't help, but for other models it can be useful. 

You can try the above fix on the mixed effects model with normal distribution (the example model in the FANGS app), and you should notice you get better ESS values for most parameters. 

## Fix 4: A sum-to-zero constraint

Fix 2 identified $\alpha$ by giving the $b_j$ a shared prior centred on zero. That works because the prior pulls the group effects toward zero, which stops them drifting off together. But it is a *soft* constraint, the $b_j$ are only centred on zero **on average, in the prior**.

With a good number of groups that is usually enough. Twenty site effects average out and the ridge is effectively closed. With **few** groups it is often not. There is little information about $\sigma_b$, so the chains can follow the prior out to large values, and the $\alpha$-versus-$b_j$ ridge in the posterior becomes difficult for the sampler to navigate.

You can fix this problem completely by making the constraint **hard**: let all but one group effect be free, and define the last as minus the sum of the others.

Here it is for a model with four groups:

```
b[1] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
b[2] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
b[3] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
b[4] <- -(b[1] + b[2] + b[3])
```

Now the four offsets sum to exactly zero in **every** draw, not just on average. There is no longer any direction the chains can slide along, so $\alpha$ is pinned down as the unambiguous grand mean across groups. A $J$-group model needs $J-1$ free effects and one deterministic line — which is why this is a tool for a handful of groups rather than twenty.

::: callout-note
## Why not always do this?

The sum-to-zero constraint changes the interpretation of the model: the last group effect is no longer a stochastic node, so it has no prior of its own and is not shrunk in the same way as the others. With a decent number of groups the soft constraint of Fix 1 is simpler, scales without writing a line per group, and pools information more evenly.

Use Fix 4 when you have **few groups** and you find the intercept will not converge despite a sensible prior on $\sigma_b$. 
:::

## Your task

1. Fit the **broken** model and read the worst R-hat and minimum ESS from the **Summary** tab.
2. Try the block sampler
3. Try each other fix in turn and record the ESS and R-hat values. 

::: callout-note
## Don't expect perfect diagnostics for this data

Even with the above fixes, at the default sampler settings the ESS are still low for some parameters and there is some variation among runs. This is a sign the chains have not settled.

Five of the twenty sites in this data have **zero** coral cover on every transect. Their $b_j$ are held finite by the shared prior and individually converge well , but they sit far below the others, around $-3.3$. To accommodate that spread the model inflates $\sigma_b$ to about 3, which **widens the $\alpha$-versus-$b_j$ ridge** — so $\alpha$ ends up the worst-mixing parameter in the model.

The lesson is the Folk Theorem: the stubborn diagnostics are pointing at a modelling problem, which here is the use of this likelihood with this dataset. A response that is 43% zeros would be better modelled with a zero-inflated or negative-binomial model, not a basic Poisson.
:::
